planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; seed propagation requires 60-90 days of cold-moist stratification before it will germinate evenly.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Amur corktree is a broad, round-headed deciduous tree with distinctive thick, deeply furrowed, corky gray bark and compound, ash-like leaves that turn yellow in fall. It is dioecious -- female trees produce small black, berry-like drupes that stain pavement and self-sow readily, so choose grafted male cultivars for street or landscape planting to avoid litter and seedling spread. The bright yellow inner bark is the source of Huang Bai, one of the most widely used bark drugs in traditional Chinese medicine, traditionally prepared for damp-heat conditions; bark is harvested from mature trees using strip-and-regenerate techniques. This species has escaped cultivation and is regulated or discouraged in parts of the northeastern US, so check local invasive-species rules and favor male selections before planting.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early spring or fall and set divisions into consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in deep shade; fresh seed germinates very slowly and erratically, so division is the reliable propagation route.

directions: Plant in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade, mimicking the understory of the mixed mountain forests of Sichuan and Hubei where it is cultivated commercially. Coptis chinensis forms a low, slow-spreading evergreen groundcover of glossy, three-lobed, toothed leaflets held on short stalks above a bright yellow, bitter rhizome -- the source of the alkaloid berberine and of Huang Lian, a cornerstone heat-clearing herb in Chinese medicine. Small white star-shaped flowers appear on thin stalks in early spring before the leaf canopy fills in overhead. It is closely related to the North American native goldthreads (Coptis trifolia) but is more robust and more commonly field-grown for root harvest, which typically takes three to five years before rhizomes reach usable size.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension -- Forest Farming Program
USDA Forest Service Non-Timber Forest Products

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer or fall for a first-year basal rosette with a thickening taproot; roots are traditionally dug in autumn of the second year, before the plant bolts and sets its spiny flower heads.

directions: Grow in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun, the same open-field conditions used to field-cultivate this plant in Sichuan and Yunnan. Himalayan teasel is a coarse biennial herb grown primarily for its spindle-shaped taproot, which is dried and sliced to produce Xu Duan, a traditional Chinese medicine herb associated with tendon, bone, and joint support. Its large, prickly-veined basal leaves and bristly stems closely resemble those of its better-known relatives Dipsacus fullonum and D. sativus, but it is cultivated as a root crop rather than for its seed-head bracts, and roots are best harvested before the plant bolts and exhausts itself flowering. Like other teasels it can self-sow if seed heads are left standing, so cut spent stalks where naturalizing is unwanted.
sources: Pacific Northwest forest-farming and specialty-herb grower guides

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or divide established clumps in early spring into moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil; seed is slow and erratic to germinate, requiring cold-moist stratification, so most growers start from divisions or nursery stock.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; this upright East Asian gentian produces glossy lance-shaped leaves along stiff stems topped from late summer into fall with clusters of large, upward-facing, deep-blue trumpet flowers. Its root is the source of Long Dan, used in traditional Chinese medicine for damp-heat conditions, and in Japan the species -- called Rindou -- has long been bred into ornamental garden selections. Established clumps resent disturbance and take a season to recover after division, so divide only occasionally and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat.

planting.note: Direct-sow in early spring after the soil has warmed, or in fall for natural overwintering; young spring shoots of established plants are harvested the following year while still tender, before flower stalks elongate.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; oriental wormwood is a finely dissected, aromatic, silvery-green subshrub that forms a low rosette in its first season and sends up slender, wiry flowering stalks in its second year and beyond. The young, unopened spring shoots are harvested while tender to produce Yin Chen, a classic traditional Chinese medicine herb associated with liver and damp-heat conditions, and is also brewed as a bitter herbal tea in parts of East Asia. It is tough and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in lean, disturbed soils, but can self-sow and naturalize in warm, humid climates, so site it where spread is acceptable or remove spent flower stalks before seed sets.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct-sow outdoors in fall so seed receives natural winter cold-moist stratification; spring sowing requires 60-90 days of refrigerated moist stratification first, and germination remains slow and uneven either way.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to light shade, the limestone prairies, glades, and open rocky woods of central and eastern North America that this small native perennial calls home. Seneca snakeroot forms a compact clump of narrow, lance-shaped leaves topped in early summer by dense, narrow spikes of tiny greenish-white, pea-like flowers. Its twisted, wintergreen-scented root was the officially recognized drug Senega in 19th- and early 20th-century pharmacopeias, traditionally used as an expectorant for coughs and bronchial congestion, and it remains a minor specialty crop for herbalists today. It establishes slowly and is most reliably grown from fall-sown seed or purchased nursery plugs; roots are typically dug for harvest from plants three years old or older in fall after the foliage dies back.
